description_full: IAMGOLD Corporation, through its subsidiaries, operates as a gold producer and developer in Canada and Burkina Faso. The company's flagship project includes Côté Gold that covers an area of 596 hectares located in the Chester and Yeo Townships, district of sudbury, in northeastern Ontario. IAMGOLD Corporation was incorporated in 1990 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.
ceo_bio: Mr. Renaud  Adams P.Eng. | CEO, President & Director | Age 55 | Compensation: $1.7M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 3K people. Revenue per employee of $763K ranks in the above the sector median among Basic Materials peers, improving at 13%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $227K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Iamgold Corporation is a large-cap basic materials business with a $10.7B market cap on $2.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +44% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 1% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 14% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $849M in free cash flow — roughly 30 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.56× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.7×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Operating margins softening -1.8pp YoY — early warning on the moat
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 38% operating margin runs 29pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.93x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+36.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 54% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 65% and a beta of 1.16, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.90 vs 5y 1.36), so read it loosely.
About $84.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 74% in the 2022 bear market and 75% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 32% below its DCF fair value of $27.68, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 70%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $21.51 to $36.42 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 9.5 vs 16.5, EV/EBITDA 4.5 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 12.6 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 21% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $22.79 on average, 21% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 1% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 3.28).
It runs a 14% gross margin and converts 30% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.56x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 27pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.1x net debt to EBITDA ($421.9M of cash against $648.8M of debt), with interest covered 9.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.4, in the safe zone).
The Beneish M-score (-2.16) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 43.8% over 3 years and 18.1% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 32%).
At current returns, reinvesting 17% of profits supports about 0.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 72.6% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 11.7% on average.
Analysts expect 11.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 77%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.6% (0.4% in buybacks).
people: With about 3,741 employees, each generates about $763K of revenue, 1.2x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 12.7% a year.
That works out to $227K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.7M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
